extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent prosecution practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: MPEP guidance for Office personnel on making and supporting determinations of obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103, including the Graham factual inquiries, search scope, rationales to support rejections, and handling applicant replies and rebuttal evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory standard for obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may not be obtained ... if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made. (Editor note: applies to FITF/AIA with 'effective filing date' adjustments.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factual inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: The framework for the objective analysis is stated in Graham v. John Deere: (A) determining the scope and content of the prior art; (B) ascertaining the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; and (C) resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objective (secondary) considerations such as commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, and unexpected results must be evaluated and given weight on a case-by-case basis. The Graham factors continue to define the inquiry that controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office personnel must act as factfinders and articulate findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel fulfill the critical role of factfinder when resolving the Graham inquiries; while the ultimate determination of obviousness is legal, the underlying Graham inquiries are factual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making an obviousness rejection, examiners must ensure the written record includes findings of fact concerning the state of the art and the teachings of the references applied, and must explain how those facts support the legal conclusion. 35 U.S.C. 132 requires notification of the reasons for rejection so applicant can respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining the scope and content of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must obtain a thorough understanding of the invention by reading the specification and claims to understand what the applicant has invented and determine the scope of the claimed invention by giving the claims the 'broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once claim scope is determined, decide what to search for and where to search. See MPEP §904. The search should cover claimed subject matter and disclosed features likely to be claimed; a preferred search looks for references that provide teaching or suggestion to combine if they exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: What to search for
rubrics_metrics.description: The search should cover the claimed subject matter and should also cover the disclosed features which might reasonably be expected to be claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although a rejection need not be based on a teaching or suggestion to combine, a preferred search will be directed to finding references that provide such a teaching or suggestion if they exist (see MPEP §904.02).

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to search (analogous and nonanalogous art considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of 35 U.S.C. 103, prior art can be either in the field of applicant’s endeavor or be reasonably pertinent to the particular problem with which the applicant was concerned; prior art from other fields may be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow general search guidelines in MPEP §904 and §904.03. KSR emphasizes that a work available in one field can prompt variations in another, and examiners should consider reasonably pertinent references and analogous art (see MPEP §2141.01(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertaining differences between the claimed invention and the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascertaining the differences requires interpreting the claim language and considering both the invention and the prior art as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret claims per MPEP §2111 and consider the whole of the claimed invention and prior art. The mere existence of differences does not establish nonobviousness if those differences would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Any obviousness rejection should include, explicitly or implicitly, an indication of the level of ordinary skill in the art, as it may be used as a partial basis to resolve obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors to consider include: (1) type of problems encountered in the art; (2) prior art solutions to those problems; (3) rapidity with which innovations are made; (4) sophistication of the technology; (5) educational level of active workers. Prior art itself may sometimes reflect the appropriate level. Office personnel may rely on their technical expertise to describe the knowledge and skills of a person of ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person of ordinary skill is hypothetical and possesses ordinary creativity
rubrics_metrics.description: The person of ordinary skill in the art is a hypothetical person presumed to have known the relevant art at the time of the invention and is 'a person of ordinary creativity, not an automaton.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a person may 'fit the teachings of multiple patents together like pieces of a puzzle' and may employ inferences and creative steps that a person of ordinary skill would use. Examiners are assumed to have familiarity with the level of skill in their art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for clear articulation of reasons supporting obviousness (avoid conclusory statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejections on obviousness cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements; there must be articulated reasoning with some rational underpinning to support the legal conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR and In re Kahn require that examiners set forth factual findings and a reasoned explanation avoiding conclusory generalizations. The key is clear articulation of the reason(s) why the claimed invention would have been obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: One rationale for obviousness is combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a combination of familiar elements according to known methods does no more than yield predictable results, it is likely obvious (KSR). Use examples in MPEP §2144 to illustrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results can support a finding of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If substituting a known element yields predictable results, the combination may be obvious (see KSR descriptions and examples in MPEP §2144).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a known technique to improve similar devices in the same way
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a known technique that was used to improve one device may be obvious when used to improve similar devices in the same way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a person of ordinary skill would recognize the technique's applicability to similar devices, using the technique is obvious unless actual application is beyond ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement to yield predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a known technique to a known device (method, or product) that is ready for improvement to yield predictable results is a valid rationale for obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rationale flows from KSR's flexible approach and the 'functional approach' in Graham; support by articulating why the device was ready for such improvement and why results were predictable.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Obvious to try" — choosing from finite predictable solutions with a reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: "Obvious to try" can support obviousness where choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions would have a reasonable expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR recognized that 'obvious to try' may be appropriate in circumstances with a finite predictable set of options; examiners must explain the predictability and expectation of success and avoid using this as a mere conclusory label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known work in one field prompting predictable variations in another field
rubrics_metrics.description: Known work in one field of endeavor may prompt variations for use in either the same field or a different one based on design incentives or market forces if the variations are predictable to one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not limit consideration only to references addressing the same problem; consider reasonably pertinent art from other fields (KSR).

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching, suggestion, or motivation (TSM) may support but is not required
rubrics_metrics.description: Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led one of ordinary skill to modify or combine references is a valid rationale, but KSR rejected an overly rigid application of the TSM test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If TSM rationale exists it should be used; however, common sense and other rationales may also support obviousness. Examiners should not demand explicit record evidence of a specific hint or suggestion when a reasoned explanation using common sense suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: TSM should not be applied rigidly; allow common-sense reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: KSR overruled overly rigid/formalistic uses of TSM and endorsed a more flexible approach where common sense and the inferences a person of ordinary skill would draw are acceptable bases for obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners may rely on common sense, market design incentives, or recognition by a skilled artisan that particular variations are predictable, but must provide reasoned explanation and factual findings — not conclusory assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's reply requirements under 37 CFR 1.111(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant must distinctly and specifically point out supposed errors in the Office's action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reply must present arguments pointing out specific distinctions believed to render the claims patentable. A mere statement that the Office has not established a prima facie case or unsupported reliance on common knowledge is not substantively adequate; examiners may repeat the rejection and make the next action final (see MPEP §706.07(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of applicant's rebuttal evidence (secondary considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should consider all timely rebuttal evidence presented by the applicant when reevaluating any obviousness determination, including secondary considerations such as commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, and unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weight given to any objective evidence is case-by-case. Examiners must articulate findings of fact that support the rationale relied upon in an obviousness rejection and reconsider in view of the entire record; see MPEP §2145 and §§716–716.10 for affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of rebuttal evidence that may show nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may submit evidence or argument to demonstrate that (A) one of ordinary skill in the art could not have combined the claimed elements by known methods (e.g., due to technological difficulties); (B) the elements in combination do not merely perform the function that each element performs separately; or (C) the results of the claimed combination were unexpected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applicant presents such evidence, examiners should reconsider the initial obviousness determination in view of the entire record and review all rejections and proposed rejections to confirm continued viability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of non-prior art references to show level of skill or motivation to combine
rubrics_metrics.description: References that do not qualify as prior art because they postdate the claimed invention, or documents not widely disseminated, may be relied upon to show the level of ordinary skill in the art or to demonstrate a motivation to combine implicit in the knowledge of one of ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Postdating documents or internal drawings may be relevant to establish knowledge or motivation even if not themselves prior art (e.g., Nat'l Steel Car v. Can. Pac. Ry.; Ex parte Erlich).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specifying a particular level of skill not always necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: If the only facts of record pertaining to the level of skill in the art are found within the prior art of record, an invention may be held obvious without a specific finding of a particular level of skill where the prior art itself reflects an appropriate level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court precedent allows reliance on the prior art to reflect the appropriate skill level (e.g., Chore‑Time Equipment; Okajima v. Bourdeau).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain objectivity by ascertaining the appropriate level of ordinary skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the art is important to maintain objectivity in the obviousness inquiry so that the question is what would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill at the time of the invention — not to the inventor, a judge, layman, or a genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate factors (see In re GPAC and related cases) and evidence to tie findings to what the ordinary skilled artisan would have known and expected.
